title: Geography Lec 5
summary: Landforms are of two types: erosional and depositional; agents: rivers, wind, glaciers, sea waves and groundwater.
Wind (aeolian): pediplain, inselberg/monadnock, mushroom rock, yardang, zeugen (erosional); barchan, seif, parabolic and transverse dunes (depositional).
River: V-shaped valley, gorge, canyon, pothole, plunge pool, waterfall (youthful stage); levee, alluvial fan, braided channel, oxbow lake (mature stage); delta (old stage).
Groundwater (karst, limestone): sinkhole, uvala, lapies; in caves, stalactites (hang from roof), stalagmites (rise from floor) and pillars.
Glacier: cirque, tarn, arete, horn, hanging valley, U-shaped valley, fjord; deposits: moraine, drumlin (basket of eggs), esker, outwash plain.
Sea waves: cliff, sea cave, sea arch, sea stack (erosional); beach, spit, bar, tombolo (depositional); India's west coast is submerged, east coast is emergent.

Endogenic forces (diastrophism: orogenic, epeirogenic; volcanism, earthquakes) build landforms; exogenic forces (denudation) wear them down; fold mountains: Himalayas/Aravallis, block mountain: Vosges, rift valley: Narmada.
The Andes is the longest mountain range (Aconcagua is its highest peak); North America's highest peak is Denali/Mount McKinley; the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the longest landform.

India has 13 major ports (12 government-owned, 1 corporatised); JNPT is the largest container port, Kochi the 'Queen of the Arabian Sea', Ennore the first corporatised port, Visakhapatnam the deepest landlocked port.
Earth's layers: crust (SIAL/SIMA), mantle (SIMA), core (NIFE); discontinuities: Conrad, Moho, Repetti, Gutenberg, Lehmann.
Seismic waves: P (longitudinal, all media, fastest), S (transverse, solids only), surface waves (Rayleigh, Love) most destructive; Mercalli measures intensity, Richter measures magnitude.
Plate tectonics: convergent (destructive), divergent (constructive), transform (conservative); Wegener 1912 (Pangaea), Harry Hess 1962 (sea-floor spreading), Arthur Holmes (convection currents).
Cyclones: tropical (over seas, >27°C, Coriolis force, move east to west) vs temperate (fronts, move west to east); cold currents create deserts on western coasts.
Rocks: igneous (granite, basalt), sedimentary (fossils, limestone), metamorphic (marble, gneiss, quartzite); intrusive forms: batholith, dyke, sill, laccolith, phacolith, lopolith.

Solar System: Venus is the hottest and rotates in reverse, Jupiter rotates fastest, Saturn has the lowest density, Earth the highest density; Uranus discovered by Herschel; Big Bang theory by Lemaitre (1927).

mcqs.q: Landforms are mainly of which two types?
mcqs.e: Both erosional and depositional landforms are made by agents like rivers, wind, glaciers, sea waves and groundwater.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT an agent of erosion?
mcqs.e: Agents of erosion are rivers, wind, glaciers, sea waves and groundwater.

mcqs.q: Landforms created by wind are called:
mcqs.e: Wind-made landforms are called aeolian and are found mainly in deserts.

mcqs.q: In deserts, the wearing down of rocks by the impact of sand particles is called:
mcqs.e: Repeated striking by wind-blown sand grains wears rocks down; this is abrasion.

mcqs.q: Which desert landform is formed by the parallel retreat of slopes (backwasting)?
mcqs.e: A pediplain is a nearly flat desert surface formed by the backwasting of slopes; stalagmites are formed by groundwater.

mcqs.q: An isolated residual hill left standing on a pediplain is called:
mcqs.e: An isolated hill left after erosion is called an inselberg or monadnock.

mcqs.q: A nearly flat plain formed by river erosion (the final stage of the erosion cycle) is called:
mcqs.e: A peneplain is made by running water; a pediplain is a desert landform.

mcqs.q: How is a mushroom rock formed in deserts?
o: By greater erosion at the top
By greater wind abrasion near the base
mcqs.e: Heavy sand moves close to the ground, so abrasion is greater at the base, leaving a narrow base and wide top.

mcqs.q: A shallow depression in a desert that temporarily fills with water is called:
mcqs.e: A playa is a shallow desert basin in which a temporary lake forms.

mcqs.q: Which of the following landforms is formed by wind erosion?
mcqs.e: Yardangs, zeugen, mushroom rocks and pedestal rocks are formed by wind erosion.

mcqs.q: Crescent-shaped sand dunes, such as those in the Thar, are called:
mcqs.e: The two horns of a barchan point in the direction of the wind.

mcqs.q: A long sand dune with a single wing, lying parallel to the wind, is called:
mcqs.e: A barchan has two horns, whereas a seif has only one.

mcqs.q: Dunes whose arms point against the wind direction because of vegetation are called:
mcqs.e: Vegetation anchors the sand, so the arms of parabolic dunes trail upwind.

mcqs.q: Sand dunes formed at right angles to the wind direction are called:
mcqs.e: Long dunes perpendicular to the wind are transverse dunes.

mcqs.q: Barchans, seifs and transverse dunes are which type of landforms?
mcqs.e: Sand dunes are formed by deposition, whereas yardangs and inselbergs are erosional.

mcqs.q: When a river cuts through rocks to form a narrow, steep-sided passage, what is formed?
mcqs.e: Vertical cutting by a river forms a gorge; plains are formed by deposition.

mcqs.q: What is the characteristic feature of a canyon?
o: A deep valley with steep, step-like walls
A plain with a wide flat floor
mcqs.e: A canyon is a large form of gorge with steep, step-like sides.

mcqs.q: Which landform is usually formed in the youthful stage of a river?
mcqs.e: In the youthful stage fast flow causes erosion, forming V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, gorges and potholes.

mcqs.q: Small circular hollows formed in the rocky bed of a river are called:
mcqs.e: Potholes are small hollows in the river bed; a plunge pool lies at the foot of a waterfall.

mcqs.q: The deep hollow formed at the base of a waterfall is called:
mcqs.e: Water falling from a height scours out a plunge pool.

mcqs.q: A waterfall in which water drops vertically from a height is called:
mcqs.e: In a plunge, water falls straight down; a cascade falls over a series of steps.

mcqs.q: What identifies a cascade waterfall?
o: Falling straight down in a single drop
Falling over a series of steps
mcqs.e: A cascade descends in multiple step-like stages.

mcqs.q: Which waterfall is called a cataract?
o: One carrying a very large volume of water
mcqs.e: In a cataract a huge volume of water falls over a series of steps.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a depositional fluvial landform?
mcqs.e: A gorge is formed by erosion; the others by deposition.

mcqs.q: The raised strip formed by sediment deposited along river banks after floods is called:
mcqs.e: When floodwater recedes, sediment is deposited along the banks, forming levees.

mcqs.q: The fan-shaped deposit laid down by a river where it descends from mountains onto a plain is called:
mcqs.e: When the slope suddenly decreases, the river drops its load in a fan shape.

mcqs.q: River channels that repeatedly split and rejoin around sandbars are called:
mcqs.e: Deposited sediment splits the stream into many interlacing channels.

mcqs.q: A plateau surrounded on all sides by mountains is called:
mcqs.e: The Tibetan Plateau, surrounded by the Himalayas and other ranges, is an intermontane plateau.

mcqs.q: Which is the highest plateau in the world?
mcqs.e: The Tibetan Plateau is the world's highest plateau.

mcqs.q: What is the main feature of a plateau?
o: An elevated landmass with a flat top
mcqs.e: A plateau has a flat top, unlike the pointed top of a mountain.

mcqs.q: Landforms created by groundwater are called:
mcqs.e: Groundwater forms karst topography in soluble rocks like limestone and dolomite.

mcqs.q: The term 'karst' comes from a region near the Adriatic Sea. Which one?
mcqs.e: The Karst region lies near the Adriatic Sea in the Balkans.

mcqs.q: Karst landforms develop in which rocks?
mcqs.e: Groundwater dissolves soluble rocks to form karst features.

mcqs.q: A large depression in limestone regions formed by the collapse of the surface is called:
mcqs.e: Groundwater-formed depressions are called swallow holes, sinkholes and collapse sinks.

mcqs.q: A valley formed when several sinkholes merge is called:
mcqs.e: The merging of several sinkholes forms a long valley called an uvala.

mcqs.q: The sharp, rough grooves and ridges formed on limestone surfaces are called:
mcqs.e: Lapies and limestone pavements are erosional karst features.

mcqs.q: The calcium carbonate structure hanging from the roof of a cave is called:
mcqs.e: Stalactites hang from the roof ('c' for ceiling).

mcqs.q: The calcium carbonate structure rising from the floor of a cave is called:
mcqs.e: Stalagmites grow upward from the floor ('g' for ground).

mcqs.q: What is formed when a stalactite and a stalagmite join together?
mcqs.e: When the two meet, a pillar or column forms in the cave.

mcqs.q: A rock layer that stores groundwater is called:
mcqs.e: An aquifer is a rock layer in which groundwater is stored.

mcqs.q: Which pair is formed by deposition inside limestone caves?
mcqs.e: Dripping water inside caves forms stalactites and stalagmites; the others are glacial or fluvial.

mcqs.q: When a glacier widens, deepens and smooths a pre-existing river valley, which valley is formed?
mcqs.e: V-shaped valleys are made by rivers; U-shaped valleys by glaciers.

mcqs.q: A semi-circular, armchair-like hollow formed by glacial erosion is called:
mcqs.e: A glacier scoops out the mountainside to form a cirque.

mcqs.q: A lake formed when water fills a cirque is called:
mcqs.e: Melting ice in a cirque forms a tarn lake.

mcqs.q: A sharp, knife-edged ridge formed between two cirques is called:
mcqs.e: An arete is a sharp ridge; several cirques together form a horn.

mcqs.q: A sharp pyramidal peak formed where three or more cirques meet is called:
mcqs.e: The Matterhorn in the Alps is a famous example of a horn.

mcqs.q: A tributary valley left hanging above a main glacial valley is called:
mcqs.e: The main valley is deepened more, leaving the tributary valley hanging above it.

mcqs.q: Which coastal feature is formed when sea water floods a glacial valley?
mcqs.e: Fjords form when the sea floods glacial valleys, as in Norway.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an erosional glacial landform?
mcqs.e: Cirques, aretes, horns, tarns and hanging valleys are erosional; moraines, eskers and drumlins are depositional.

mcqs.q: Which group correctly lists depositional glacial landforms?
mcqs.e: Moraines, eskers, drumlins and outwash plains are glacial deposits.

mcqs.q: Which landform gives rise to 'basket of eggs' topography?
mcqs.e: Groups of drumlins look like inverted boats or a basket of eggs.

mcqs.q: Debris deposited along the sides of a glacier is called:
mcqs.e: Deposits along the sides are lateral moraines; those in the middle are medial moraines.

mcqs.q: A steep rocky wall formed by the erosion of sea waves is called:
mcqs.e: Waves pounding the coast form cliffs.

mcqs.q: A rock pillar standing detached from the coast is called:
mcqs.e: A sea stack forms when the roof of an arch collapses.

mcqs.q: When wave erosion hollows a rock right through, what is formed?
mcqs.e: A hole right through forms an arch; a hollow only partly inward is a sea cave.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a depositional coastal landform?
mcqs.e: Beaches, spits, bars and tombolos are formed by deposition.

mcqs.q: A sand bar connecting an island to the mainland is called:
mcqs.e: A tombolo is a strip of sand linking an island to the mainland.

mcqs.q: Long sand dunes parallel to the coast form most commonly on:
mcqs.e: Depositional features dominate on low sedimentary (emergent) coasts.

mcqs.q: India's western coastal plain is an example of which type of coast?
mcqs.e: The west coast is submerged, hence narrow and suited to natural harbours.

mcqs.q: What is India's eastern coastal plain like?
mcqs.e: The east coast is broad, emergent and depositional.

mcqs.q: Why are there few natural harbours on the eastern coastal plain?
o: It is close to the Equator
mcqs.e: Emergent coasts have shallow water, so natural harbours are few.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of young fold mountains?
mcqs.e: The Himalayas are young fold mountains; the Aravallis are old (residual) fold mountains.

mcqs.q: Fold mountains are formed by the folding of which rocks?
mcqs.e: Compressional forces fold sedimentary layers to form fold mountains.

mcqs.q: Which old fold mountains lie in the eastern part of North America?
mcqs.e: The Appalachians are old fold mountains; the Rockies are young fold mountains.

mcqs.q: The Vosges mountains in France are of which type?
mcqs.e: The Vosges are block mountains; the Alps and Rockies are fold mountains.

mcqs.q: Geomorphic processes are mainly divided into which two categories?
mcqs.e: Endogenic forces build from within; exogenic forces wear down from outside.

mcqs.q: The endogenic process that builds landforms is called:
mcqs.e: Diastrophism builds relief; denudation wears landforms down.

mcqs.q: The process of mountain building is called:
mcqs.e: 'Oros' means mountain; orogeny is mountain building.

mcqs.q: The process of uplift of large parts of the Earth's crust is called:
mcqs.e: Epeirogeny involves uplift of areas far larger than mountains.

mcqs.q: What is the main source of energy for exogenic forces?
mcqs.e: Solar heat drives wind, running water and glaciers.

mcqs.q: The sunken block between two faults is called:
mcqs.e: The uplifted block is called a horst (block mountain).

mcqs.q: The Narmada flows between the Vindhyas and the Satpuras through which structure?
mcqs.e: The Narmada flows westward through a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges.

mcqs.q: Which mountain range is located in South America?
mcqs.e: The Andes run along the western coast of South America.

mcqs.q: Which is the longest mountain range in the world?
mcqs.e: The Andes, about 7,000 km long, are the world's longest continental mountain range.

mcqs.q: Which is the highest peak in South America?
mcqs.e: Aconcagua lies in the Andes in Argentina.

mcqs.q: Which is the highest peak of North America?
mcqs.e: Denali, also called Mount McKinley, lies in the Alaska Range in Alaska.

mcqs.q: The grasslands of Venezuela are called:
mcqs.e: Campos are the grasslands of Brazil.

mcqs.q: Shifting cultivation in Brazil is known as:
mcqs.e: In India it is called jhum.

mcqs.q: Which is the largest container port in India?
mcqs.e: JNPT near Mumbai is also a satellite port of Mumbai.

mcqs.q: What is a satellite port?
o: A port built to relieve a nearby port that has reached capacity
A port located on an island
A port used only for fishing
mcqs.e: JNPT was built when Mumbai port reached its capacity.

mcqs.q: Deendayal (Kandla) Port is what type of port?
mcqs.e: Kandla is in Gujarat and depends on tides.

mcqs.q: Mormugao Port is located at the mouth of which river?
mcqs.e: Mormugao (Goa) is a major iron-ore exporting port.

mcqs.q: Which port is called the 'Queen of the Arabian Sea'?
mcqs.e: Kochi is in Kerala.

mcqs.q: Which was India's first corporatised major port?
mcqs.e: Ennore is in Tamil Nadu.

mcqs.q: Which is the deepest landlocked port in India?
mcqs.e: Visakhapatnam is in Andhra Pradesh.

mcqs.q: Paradip Port is in which state?
mcqs.e: Paradip is the major port of Odisha.

mcqs.q: Which is the oldest major port of India?
mcqs.e: Kolkata is a riverine port.

mcqs.q: How many major ports does India have?
mcqs.e: Of the 13 major ports, 12 are government-owned and 1 is corporatised.

mcqs.q: Major ports are under the control of:
mcqs.e: Minor ports are under state governments.

mcqs.q: Which are the three major ports of Tamil Nadu?
mcqs.e: All three are on the east coast.

mcqs.q: Tides are caused by which forces?
o: Gravitational pull of the Sun and Moon and centrifugal force
mcqs.e: Along with gravitation, centrifugal force also causes tides.

mcqs.q: When do spring tides occur?
o: When the three bodies are at 90°
When the Earth is farthest from the Sun
When the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a straight line (syzygy)
mcqs.e: At syzygy, high tides are very high and low tides very low.

mcqs.q: When do neap tides occur?
o: When the three bodies are in a straight line
When the three bodies are in quadrature (90°)
mcqs.e: The tidal range is small during neap tides.

mcqs.q: How many high tides occur in a day in a diurnal tide?
mcqs.e: A semi-diurnal tide has two high and two low tides a day.

mcqs.q: The duration of a diurnal tidal cycle is about:
mcqs.e: A lunar day is about 24 hours 50 minutes long.

mcqs.q: A tree-branch-like drainage pattern, common in the northern plains, is called:
mcqs.e: Tributaries join the main river like branches of a tree.

mcqs.q: The Narmada and Son rising from Amarkantak is an example of which drainage pattern?
mcqs.e: In a radial pattern rivers flow outward in all directions from a central high point.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of a centripetal drainage pattern?
mcqs.e: Rivers drain into a central depression.

mcqs.q: Which is the world's only floating national park?
mcqs.e: It lies on Loktak Lake in Manipur.

mcqs.q: In a trellis drainage pattern, how do tributaries join the main river?
mcqs.e: In a trellis pattern secondary tributaries join at right angles.

mcqs.q: Which landform results from the winding course of a river on a plain?
mcqs.e: When a meander is cut off, an oxbow lake forms.

mcqs.q: What are the main causes of river meandering?
mcqs.e: On the gentle slopes of plains a river winds from side to side.

mcqs.q: What is the correct order of the three stages of a river?
mcqs.e: Deltas form in the old stage.

mcqs.q: An entrenched meander is what type of landform?
mcqs.e: It forms when a river cuts deep into rock along its meandering course.

mcqs.q: High waves generated by an undersea earthquake are called:
mcqs.e: Tsunami is a Japanese word meaning 'harbour waves'.

mcqs.q: By volume, which is the largest part of the Earth?
mcqs.e: The crust is about 1% and the core about 15% of Earth's volume.

mcqs.q: The continental crust is made of:
mcqs.e: Continental crust is thicker but less dense.

mcqs.q: The oceanic crust is made of:
mcqs.e: Oceanic crust is thinner but denser.

mcqs.q: The Earth's core is made of:
mcqs.e: Ni = nickel, Fe = ferrum (iron).

mcqs.q: The crust and the upper solid part of the mantle together are called:
mcqs.e: The lithosphere is broken into tectonic plates.

mcqs.q: What is the asthenosphere like?
mcqs.e: Lithospheric plates move over it.

mcqs.q: Which layer is responsible for the Earth's magnetic field?
mcqs.e: The liquid outer core, together with Earth's rotation, generates the magnetic field.

mcqs.q: Why is the inner core solid?
mcqs.e: The outer core, under less pressure, is liquid.

mcqs.q: The point of origin of an earthquake is called:
mcqs.e: The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it.

mcqs.q: What is the epicentre of an earthquake?
o: The surface point that waves reach first and where damage is greatest
A point found only in the sea
mcqs.e: It lies on the surface directly above the hypocentre.

mcqs.q: Seismic waves are mainly divided into which two categories?
mcqs.e: Body waves include P and S waves.

mcqs.q: Which wave travels through solids, liquids and gases?
mcqs.e: P waves are the fastest and arrive first.

mcqs.q: S waves travel through:
mcqs.e: S waves cannot pass through the liquid outer core.

mcqs.q: What is the nature of P waves?
mcqs.e: They cause compression and rarefaction of the medium.

mcqs.q: What is the nature of S waves?
mcqs.e: They form crests and troughs.

mcqs.q: Which seismic waves are the most destructive?
mcqs.e: Surface waves travel along the Earth's surface.

mcqs.q: What are the two types of surface waves?
mcqs.e: Rayleigh waves roll; Love waves move side to side.

mcqs.q: The region where S waves are not recorded is called:
mcqs.e: The S-wave shadow zone is much larger than the P-wave shadow zone.

mcqs.q: The P-wave shadow zone lies roughly between:
mcqs.e: The S-wave shadow zone covers everything beyond 105°.

mcqs.q: The intensity of an earthquake is measured on which scale?
mcqs.e: The Mercalli scale ranges from I to XII.

mcqs.q: What does the Richter scale measure?
mcqs.e: It has no theoretical upper limit.

mcqs.q: Which instrument records seismic waves?
mcqs.e: An anemometer measures wind speed.

mcqs.q: At about what depth is the mantle-core boundary?
mcqs.e: The Earth's radius is about 6,400 km.

mcqs.q: Which discontinuity lies between the mantle and the core?
mcqs.e: Order from surface: Conrad, Moho, Repetti, Gutenberg, Lehmann.

mcqs.q: Which discontinuity lies between the crust and the mantle?
mcqs.e: The Mohorovicic discontinuity is the crust-mantle boundary.

mcqs.q: Which discontinuity lies between the upper and lower crust?
mcqs.e: The Repetti discontinuity lies between the upper and lower mantle.

mcqs.q: Which discontinuity lies between the outer and inner core?
mcqs.e: Lehmann is the deepest of the major discontinuities.

mcqs.q: How were the Himalayas formed?
o: By the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates
mcqs.e: Sediments of the Tethys Sea were compressed and folded.

mcqs.q: What kind of boundary is a convergent plate boundary?
mcqs.e: The denser plate sinks and melts.

mcqs.q: What kind of boundary is a divergent plate boundary?
mcqs.e: Magma rises to form new crust.

mcqs.q: A transform plate boundary is also called a:
mcqs.e: Plates slide past each other without creating or destroying crust.

mcqs.q: When an oceanic plate and a continental plate collide, which one sinks?
mcqs.e: Being denser, the oceanic plate sinks; this is called a subduction zone.

mcqs.q: Which is the longest landform in the world?
mcqs.e: It lies along a divergent plate boundary.

mcqs.q: Who proposed the theory of sea-floor spreading?
mcqs.e: Harry Hess proposed it in 1962.

mcqs.q: Who proposed the Continental Drift theory, and when?
mcqs.e: Wegener was a German meteorologist.

mcqs.q: What name did Wegener give to the single giant landmass?
mcqs.e: Panthalassa was the single global ocean.

mcqs.q: Pangaea split into which two parts?
mcqs.e: Laurasia lay to the north and Gondwanaland to the south.

mcqs.q: Which of the following was NOT evidence for Wegener's drift theory?
mcqs.e: Matching gold-bearing deposits (placer deposits) were also cited as evidence.

mcqs.q: Which forces did Wegener propose for drift, later found inadequate?
mcqs.e: Convection currents were later accepted as the driving mechanism.

mcqs.q: Who proposed convection currents as the cause of plate movement?
mcqs.e: Holmes proposed mantle convection in the 1930s.

mcqs.q: Where do convection currents get their energy from?
mcqs.e: They are driven by the Earth's internal heat.

mcqs.q: The peeling off of the outer layers of rock like onion skins due to temperature changes is called:
mcqs.e: It is a form of mechanical weathering.

mcqs.q: Carbonation is which type of weathering?
mcqs.e: Carbonic acid formed from CO2 and water dissolves the rock.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT chemical weathering?
mcqs.e: Frost wedging is mechanical weathering.

mcqs.q: Why is weathering called an 'in situ' process?
o: The rock breaks down in its original place
The rock is carried far away
Wind lifts and carries it away
mcqs.e: Weathering involves no transportation of material.

mcqs.q: Breaking of rocks by tree roots or animals is which type of weathering?
mcqs.e: Rodents, snakes and plant roots are biological agents.

mcqs.q: Which weathering dominates in karst landforms?
mcqs.e: Groundwater dissolves limestone.

mcqs.q: What is the main cause of V-shaped valleys in mountain areas?
mcqs.e: Glaciers form U-shaped valleys.

mcqs.q: Which statement about volcanism is correct?
o: It creates new landforms on the surface
It is controlled only by rainfall
mcqs.e: It is an endogenic process.

mcqs.q: The large-scale downslope movement of rock or soil under gravity is called:
mcqs.e: Weathering helps but is not a prerequisite for mass movement.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a rapid mass movement?
mcqs.e: Landslides, avalanches and mudflows are rapid movements.

mcqs.q: The slow downslope flow of water-saturated soil is called:
mcqs.e: Solifluction is slow; a slump involves debris rotating backward as it slides.

mcqs.q: Where do landslides generally occur most?
mcqs.e: The Himalayan region is highly prone to landslides.

mcqs.q: Which continent is called the 'island continent'?
mcqs.e: Australia is a continent surrounded by water on all sides.

mcqs.q: An interconnected submarine mountain chain in the oceans, with a central rift and volcanoes, is called:
mcqs.e: It forms at divergent plate boundaries where sea-floor spreading occurs.

mcqs.q: Which is the first part of the ocean floor from the coast, with a gentle slope of 1° or less?
mcqs.e: Petroleum and minerals are extracted from the shelf.

mcqs.q: What is the correct order of ocean floor features from the coast towards the deep sea?
mcqs.e: Abyssal plains are also called deep-sea plains.

mcqs.q: A flat-topped submerged mountain in the ocean is called:
mcqs.e: A pointed submerged mountain is a seamount; a flat-topped one is a guyot.

mcqs.q: A ring-shaped coral reef is called:
mcqs.e: Atolls are ring-shaped coral reefs, as found in Lakshadweep.

mcqs.q: Which continent has the highest average elevation?
mcqs.e: Its thick ice sheet gives Antarctica the highest average elevation; it is called the White Continent.

mcqs.q: Which continent has the largest number of countries?
mcqs.e: Africa has 54 countries, the most of any continent.

mcqs.q: Which is the highest peak in Africa?
mcqs.e: Kilimanjaro, a volcanic mountain, is in Tanzania.

mcqs.q: Which mountain range lies in northern Africa?
mcqs.e: The Atlas Mountains are in north-west Africa.

mcqs.q: In oceanography, what does 'halocline' mean?
o: A sharp change in temperature with depth
A decrease in density with depth
A sharp change in salinity with depth
A change in pressure with depth
mcqs.e: 'Halo' means salt; in a thermocline temperature falls sharply with depth.

mcqs.q: What is a thermocline?
o: A layer where temperature falls rapidly with depth
mcqs.e: 'Thermo' means heat; the thermocline is the layer of rapid temperature decrease.

mcqs.q: Which ocean has the largest number of trenches?
mcqs.e: The Pacific has about 32 trenches, the Indian Ocean only about 6.

mcqs.q: Which is the deepest trench in the world?
mcqs.e: The Mariana Trench in the Pacific is about 11 km deep.

mcqs.q: Which is the deepest trench in the Indian Ocean?
mcqs.e: The Sunda (Java) Trench is the deepest in the Indian Ocean, over 7,000 m.

mcqs.q: For a tropical cyclone to form, the sea surface temperature should be about:
mcqs.e: A large warm sea surface, low pressure and the Coriolis force are needed.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a condition for the formation of tropical cyclones?
mcqs.e: Warm water is needed, not a cold current.

mcqs.q: The Coriolis effect is also expressed as:
mcqs.e: The Coriolis force arises from the Earth's rotation.

mcqs.q: Where is the Coriolis force maximum and where is it zero?
o: Maximum at the Equator, zero at the poles
Maximum at the poles, zero at the Equator
mcqs.e: It increases with latitude.

mcqs.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, the Coriolis force deflects winds and currents to the:
mcqs.e: In the Southern Hemisphere they are deflected to the left.

mcqs.q: What is the characteristic of the eye of a cyclone?
mcqs.e: The eye is surrounded by a wall of cumulonimbus clouds.

mcqs.q: Which clouds mainly form in a cyclone?
mcqs.e: They have great vertical development and an anvil-shaped top.

mcqs.q: Which grey clouds block sunlight and cause heavy rain?
mcqs.e: Nimbus clouds are dark, dense clouds that bring heavy rain.

mcqs.q: Which clouds have a flat base and a cauliflower-like shape?
mcqs.e: Cumulus clouds look like cotton wool.

mcqs.q: Which feathery, high-altitude clouds are made of ice crystals?
mcqs.e: Cirrus clouds occur at high altitudes of about 8-12 km.

mcqs.q: In which direction does a cyclone rotate in the Northern Hemisphere?
mcqs.e: In the Southern Hemisphere cyclones rotate clockwise.

mcqs.q: An anticyclone forms around which pressure area?
mcqs.e: High pressure brings clear, fair weather.

mcqs.q: What is the direction of an anticyclone in the Northern Hemisphere?
mcqs.e: Opposite to a cyclone; anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

mcqs.q: How are temperate cyclones formed?
o: By front formation when warm and cold air masses meet
mcqs.e: They form by frontogenesis in mid-latitudes and can occur over both land and sea.

mcqs.q: In which direction do tropical cyclones move?
mcqs.e: They move east to west with the trade winds; temperate cyclones move west to east with the westerlies.

mcqs.q: Where do tropical cyclones form?
mcqs.e: Temperate cyclones can form over both land and sea.

mcqs.q: What happens in an occluded front?
o: Warm air pushes cold air down
Cold air lifts the warm air completely off the ground
mcqs.e: Cold air, being heavier, stays below and the warm air is lifted up.

mcqs.q: Who names tropical cyclones?
o: WMO and ESCAP (from lists of regional countries)
mcqs.e: Names for the north Indian Ocean come from member countries under the WMO/ESCAP Panel.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a factor affecting ocean currents?
mcqs.e: Insolation, density, gravity and the Coriolis force affect ocean currents.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a cold ocean current?
mcqs.e: Benguela, Canary, California, Peru, Labrador and Falkland are cold currents.

mcqs.q: The Canary Current is in which ocean?
mcqs.e: The cold Canary Current flows off the north-west coast of Africa in the Atlantic.

mcqs.q: Which is the driest desert in the world, and which current is it linked to?
mcqs.e: The Atacama (Chile-Peru) is the world's driest desert.

mcqs.q: The Namib Desert has formed because of which cold current?
mcqs.e: The Benguela Current flows along the south-west coast of Africa.

mcqs.q: Why are deserts mostly found on the western coasts of continents?
mcqs.e: Cold air holds less moisture, so rainfall is low.

mcqs.q: What forms where warm and cold ocean currents meet?
mcqs.e: Examples are Newfoundland (Grand Banks) and Japan; fog, however, hampers ports there.

mcqs.q: The meeting of the Oyashio and Kuroshio currents creates a fishing ground near:
mcqs.e: Warm and cold currents meet here to create rich fishing grounds.

mcqs.q: Which warm current moderates the climate of Western Europe?
mcqs.e: The North Atlantic Drift, an extension of the Gulf Stream, keeps Western Europe warm.

mcqs.q: A large circular system of ocean currents is called a:
mcqs.e: Large-scale ocean circulation loops are called gyres.

mcqs.q: Which current flows eastward between the North and South Equatorial Currents?
mcqs.e: It flows near the Equator in the opposite direction.

mcqs.q: What is the main destructive force of a tropical storm in coastal areas?
mcqs.e: The rise of sea water onto the coast during a cyclone is the most destructive.

mcqs.q: Which of the following does NOT affect the horizontal distribution of air pressure?
mcqs.e: Temperature, altitude and rotation affect air pressure; salinity does not.

mcqs.q: Which river creates a fertile area in the Thar (Great Indian Desert)?
mcqs.e: The Ghaggar flows through Haryana and Rajasthan.

mcqs.q: What is the evidence that the Thar was under the sea in the Mesozoic era?
mcqs.e: These show that the region was once under the sea.

mcqs.q: The 'Ring of Fire' is located in which ocean?
mcqs.e: Convergent plate boundaries here cause most earthquakes and volcanoes.

mcqs.q: What is the shape of the Ring of Fire?
mcqs.e: It is a horseshoe-shaped belt around the Pacific rim, including Japan and Indonesia.

mcqs.q: A volcano with a layered structure is also called a:
mcqs.e: Composite volcanoes have thick lava and steep slopes.

mcqs.q: In which volcano does very fluid lava spread far, giving gentle slopes?
mcqs.e: Fluid basaltic lava forms gentle slopes.

mcqs.q: Which is the most explosive type of volcano?
mcqs.e: In a caldera, the volcano collapses into itself after a violent eruption.

mcqs.q: The bowl-shaped depression at the mouth of a volcano is called:
mcqs.e: The vent is the passage through which lava emerges; the depression at the top is the crater.

mcqs.q: What is the characteristic of acidic lava?
mcqs.e: Composite volcanoes usually have acidic, viscous lava.

mcqs.q: Rocks formed by the solidification of magma inside the Earth are called:
mcqs.e: Intrusive igneous rocks form below the surface.

mcqs.q: A huge dome-shaped mass formed when magma solidifies in the magma chamber itself is called:
mcqs.e: A batholith is the largest dome-shaped intrusive body.

mcqs.q: A vertical igneous intrusion is called a:
mcqs.e: A dyke is vertical; a sill is horizontal.

mcqs.q: An igneous intrusion solidified between horizontal layers is called a:
mcqs.e: A sill lies horizontally between rock layers.

mcqs.q: Which dome-shaped intrusive body is connected to a pipe-like conduit?
mcqs.e: A laccolith has a flat base and a domed top, fed by a conduit.

mcqs.q: An igneous body lying in a wavy form along anticlines and synclines is called a:
mcqs.e: A phacolith is a wavy intrusive body.

mcqs.q: A saucer-shaped intrusive igneous body, concave towards the sky, is called a:
mcqs.e: A lopolith is saucer-shaped with a sunken centre.

mcqs.q: Rocks are mainly of how many types?
mcqs.e: Three types: igneous (primary), sedimentary and metamorphic.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of igneous rock?
mcqs.e: Granite, basalt, gabbro and pumice are igneous rocks.

mcqs.q: The oceanic crust is mainly made of which rock?
mcqs.e: Oceanic crust is basaltic; continental crust is granitic.

mcqs.q: In which rocks are fossils found?
mcqs.e: Sedimentary rocks form in layers, so fossils are preserved in them.

mcqs.q: The process by which sedimentary rocks are formed is called:
mcqs.e: In lithification, sediments are compacted into rock.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of sedimentary rock?
mcqs.e: Limestone, sandstone and chalk are sedimentary rocks.

mcqs.q: Which rock is formed by the metamorphism of limestone?
mcqs.e: Sandstone changes to quartzite and granite to gneiss.

mcqs.q: Which rock is formed by the metamorphism of granite?
mcqs.e: Gneiss is the metamorphosed form of granite.

mcqs.q: What is formed by the metamorphism of sandstone?
mcqs.e: Metamorphic rocks include marble, quartzite, slate and gneiss.

mcqs.q: The arrangement of minerals in lines or layers during metamorphism is called:
mcqs.e: In banding, alternating light and dark bands form.

mcqs.q: The continuous process by which one rock changes into another is called:
mcqs.e: In the rock cycle, igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks keep transforming into one another.

mcqs.q: What are the three types of sedimentary rocks by mode of formation?
mcqs.e: Mechanically formed sedimentary rocks are called clastic.

mcqs.q: Victoria is the capital of which country?
mcqs.e: Port Louis is the capital of Mauritius, Antananarivo of Madagascar and Moroni of Comoros.

mcqs.q: Mont Blanc is the highest peak of which mountain range?
mcqs.e: Everest tops the Himalayas, Aconcagua the Andes and Anamudi the Western Ghats.

mcqs.q: Which strait separates India from Sri Lanka?
mcqs.e: The Palk Strait connects the Bay of Bengal with Palk Bay.

mcqs.q: The Strait of Hormuz connects which two water bodies?
o: Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman
Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal
mcqs.e: A strait connects two large water bodies and separates two landmasses.

mcqs.q: Which is the southernmost nuclear power plant in India?
mcqs.e: Kudankulam is in the far south of Tamil Nadu.

mcqs.q: The Kakrapar Atomic Power Station is in which state?
mcqs.e: Narora is in Uttar Pradesh and Kaiga in Karnataka.

mcqs.q: Which is the oldest nuclear power plant in India?
mcqs.e: Tarapur (Maharashtra) began operating in 1969.

mcqs.q: In nuclear fission, what is mainly produced when a neutron strikes uranium?
mcqs.e: Fission of U-235 releases barium, krypton and three neutrons, sustaining a chain reaction.

mcqs.q: What is used in a nuclear reactor to slow down neutrons?
mcqs.e: Control rods are made of cadmium or boron.

mcqs.q: Control rods of a nuclear reactor are made of:
mcqs.e: They absorb neutrons to control the chain reaction.

mcqs.q: What causes convectional rainfall?
o: Air rising due to intense surface heating
Meeting of cold and warm air
mcqs.e: Rising warm moist air cools, forms clouds and causes rain.

mcqs.q: Rainfall caused when air rises along a mountain barrier is called:
mcqs.e: Monsoon rainfall on the Western Ghats is orographic.

mcqs.q: Rainfall caused by temperate cyclones is called:
mcqs.e: Frontal rain occurs where cold and warm air masses meet.

mcqs.q: Pre-monsoon convectional thunderstorms (such as Nor'westers / Kalbaisakhi) mainly occur in:
mcqs.e: Pre-monsoon thundershowers here are called Nor'westers.

mcqs.q: Who proposed the Big Bang theory of the origin of the universe?
mcqs.e: Georges Lemaitre proposed it in 1927.

mcqs.q: Who proposed the nebular hypothesis of the origin of the Solar System (from a rotating cloud of gas and dust)?
mcqs.e: It is known as the Kant-Laplace nebular hypothesis.

mcqs.q: How many planets are there in the Solar System?
mcqs.e: There are eight planets; Ceres is a dwarf planet in the asteroid belt.

mcqs.q: The asteroid belt lies between which two planets?
mcqs.e: The asteroid belt separates the terrestrial and Jovian planets.

mcqs.q: The inner planets are called:
mcqs.e: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are rocky, dense terrestrial planets.

mcqs.q: What is the density of the outer (Jovian) planets like?
o: Low, as they are made of gases
mcqs.e: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are large but low-density gas/ice planets.

mcqs.q: The Galilean moons belong to which planet?
mcqs.e: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto were discovered by Galileo.

mcqs.q: Which is the largest moon in the Solar System?
mcqs.e: Ganymede is a moon of Jupiter; Titan is Saturn's famous moon.

mcqs.q: Which is a famous moon of Saturn?
mcqs.e: Titan is Saturn's largest moon.

mcqs.q: Which planet completes its revolution around the Sun in the shortest time (about 88 days)?
mcqs.e: Mercury is closest to the Sun; Neptune takes about 165 years.

mcqs.q: Which planet takes the longest time (about 165 years) to revolve around the Sun?
mcqs.e: Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun.

mcqs.q: Which planet rotates on its axis in the shortest time?
mcqs.e: Jupiter rotates once in about 9 hours 55 minutes.

mcqs.q: Which planet takes the longest time (about 243 days) to rotate on its axis?
mcqs.e: Venus has the slowest rotation.

mcqs.q: Which planet is called Earth's twin?
mcqs.e: Venus is also called the Morning Star and the Evening Star.

mcqs.q: Which is the hottest and brightest planet in the Solar System?
mcqs.e: Thick sulphuric acid clouds and the greenhouse effect trap heat on Venus.

mcqs.q: Which two planets rotate from east to west?
mcqs.e: All other planets rotate from west to east.

mcqs.q: Which planet is called the 'rolling planet'?
mcqs.e: Uranus's axis is tilted by about 98°.

mcqs.q: Which planet has the lowest density, even less than water?
mcqs.e: Saturn's density is about 0.69 g/cm³, less than water.

mcqs.q: Which planet has the highest density in the Solar System?
mcqs.e: Earth is the densest of all planets.

mcqs.q: What are the two moons of Mars?
mcqs.e: Iron oxide gives Mars its red colour, hence the 'Red Planet'.

mcqs.q: What percentage of the Earth's surface is covered by water and land respectively?
mcqs.e: That is why Earth is called the Blue Planet.

mcqs.q: About what percentage of the Earth's total water is fresh water?
mcqs.e: Most water is saline; most fresh water is locked in glaciers and ice caps.

mcqs.q: Where is the largest share of fresh water (about 68%) stored?
mcqs.e: Most fresh water exists as ice.

mcqs.q: Which surface has the highest albedo (reflectivity)?
mcqs.e: Freshly fallen snow reflects the most sunlight.

mcqs.q: Who discovered Uranus?
mcqs.e: William Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781.

mcqs.q: Whose names are associated with the discovery/prediction of Neptune?
mcqs.e: Le Verrier predicted Neptune and Johann Galle observed it in 1846.

mcqs.q: Which of these planets is the farthest from the Sun?
mcqs.e: Neptune is the eighth and outermost planet of the Solar System.

mcqs.q: Which planets are the cold 'ice giants'?
mcqs.e: Jupiter and Saturn are called gas giants.

mcqs.q: Where is the dwarf planet Ceres located?
mcqs.e: Ceres is a dwarf planet in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

mcqs.q: Approximately when did Arthur Holmes propose his convection current model?
mcqs.e: Wegener's theory came in 1912 and Holmes's convection model in the 1930s.

mcqs.q: Landslides and land subsidence linked to mining are more common in which type of region?
mcqs.e: Landslides associated with mining and subsidence are more frequent on mountain slopes.

mcqs.q: A sharp, wind-cut ridge in the desert aligned with the wind direction is called:
mcqs.e: A yardang is a sharp ridge parallel to the wind direction.

mcqs.q: A flat-topped, table-like rock in the desert is called:
mcqs.e: A zeugen is a tabular rock with a hard, flat cap layer.
